archetype.name: Pocket Passer (big-arm, mobile)
archetype.definition: A tall, strong-armed passer who wins from the pocket and adds real yardage with his legs. For six years he produced positive EPA per play behind volume passing, but this season the structure around him has collapsed and his own accuracy has slipped with it.

report.headline: A 0-8 season where the line, the run game and his own turnovers compound.
report.take:
Herbert's résumé is not in question. Through six seasons he never posted a negative EPA per play, he finished top 10 in passing yards in four of them, and last year he added 498 rushing yards (2nd among QBs). That is what makes 2026 so jarring. His -0.245 EPA per dropback ranks 42nd of 49, his CPOE of -5.09 ranks 42nd, and the Chargers are 0-8 with him starting every game.

The environment explains a lot of it. The offense ranks 32nd of 32 in EPA, rushing EPA and success rate. It is also the most run-heavy team in the league relative to situation, with a pass rate over expected of -11.4. The result is a QB who keeps inheriting third downs averaging 8.7 yards to go behind a line that ranks 31st in hit rate allowed. The quick game meant to bail him out has been a drain: throws behind the line have added up to -15.6 EPA. His two tight ends have been black holes at -9.2 and -11.9 EPA on their targets. Meanwhile McConkey, Johnston and Harris are all comfortably positive.

What the context doesn't cover is the turnovers and the sacks. His CPOE swung 6.7 points down from last year. Nine of his 11 interceptions came on throws of 10+ air yards, where he completes 46.4%. His pressure-to-sack rate of 36.5% is the top of a creep that has run for years: 17.1% as a rookie, 33.3% in 2024, 29.7% last year. He is pressured at a middling rate (24.4%) and still turns those pressures into sacks more than most. The damage clusters where games are decided. One-score situations account for -59.5 of his -72.5 dropback EPA. Close fourth quarters have been brutal: -32.3 EPA on 28 plays with 9 sacks. Some of that is a small, high-leverage sample that will not stay this extreme. Some of it is a quarterback pressing.

The arrow is still pointing down. His last three games came in at -0.323 EPA per dropback with a 13.2% sack rate, both worse than his season. Week 9 brought 8 sacks and only 79% of the snaps. He is now questionable with a left middle finger injury (no fracture, per Harbaugh), guard Kayode Awosika is out, and McConkey, his most efficient target, is day-to-day with back spasms. His history says the interception rate and TD rate should drift back toward normal. Nothing in the dossier says the protection or the run game is about to change.

strengths.title: The wide receivers still produce
strengths.body: When the ball goes to his wideouts, the offense works. McConkey, Johnston and Harris all carry positive EPA per target, while the tight end targets sink the totals. This is the clearest sign the arm still functions. The fix is partly distribution: more of the volume going to the receivers who are earning it.

strengths.title: Downfield throws still create value
strengths.body: Despite four interceptions on 26 deep attempts, his 20+ yard throws are net positive at +0.054 EPA. Intermediate throws succeed 46.6% of the time. The big-play ability that defined his early years hasn't vanished. It comes bundled with turnovers, and he has throttled his aggressiveness to 13.19% from 14.6% last year.

strengths.title: Legs remain a real outlet
strengths.body: His 190 rushing yards rank 7th among QBs, and scrambles are slightly positive in EPA. That follows a 2025 in which he ranked 2nd at the position in rushing yards. The mobility is durable, though designed runs have been stuffed 36.4% of the time behind this line.

concerns.title: Sacks are drowning the offense
concerns.body: An 11.7% sack rate ranks 44th of 49. The line is part of it: the offense ranks 31st in hit rate allowed. But his pressure-to-sack rate of 36.5% caps a multi-year climb, and his time to throw of 2.8 seconds isn't unusually long. That points to holding the ball and failing to escape, not just to free rushers. With Awosika out, expect this to persist.

concerns.title: Interceptions on every throw past 10
concerns.body: Nine of his 11 picks have come on throws of 10+ air yards. His CPOE on those throws is -6.7, and the intermediate band alone holds five interceptions. His career shows he has always carried some interception risk (15 in 2021, 13 last year), but a 4.7% rate is outside his norm. His accuracy is down 6.7 CPOE points from 2025. Expect some regression toward his history, though not a full reversal while he is pressing in close games.

concerns.title: A scheme that leaves him in long yardage
concerns.body: The Chargers run far more than situation suggests, yet they own the league's worst rushing EPA. That produces third downs at 8.7 yards to go, and he converts 34.9% of them. The screen and quick game behind the line, which should offset the pressure, has been the least efficient part of his passing tree. This is mostly a role and scheme problem rather than a Herbert flaw, but it isn't going away mid-season.

trend.note: Weeks 1-3 were bad but survivable. Since Week 4 his EPA per dropback has sunk further, bottoming out with -14.0 at Kansas City and -16.2 against the Rams. Week 9 brought 8 sacks on 23 attempts and a reduced 79% snap share before the finger injury report.

nextGame.headline: A thinned Ravens secondary invites the deep shots he's avoided
nextGame.body:
Baltimore's defense is middle of the pack overall (19th in EPA, 20th against the pass), and it splits sharply by depth. It is 5th in short-pass EPA allowed, which smothers the under-10 game the Chargers have leaned on. It is 26th on deep throws and 31st in EPA allowed to opposing WR1s. That is the right shape for Herbert, whose deep throws are net positive and whose wideouts are his efficient targets. The Ravens' pass rush is ordinary (21st in sack rate), which is the softest front he has seen in a while. With Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley both on IR, a low 38.5 total and a 5.5-point spread suggest a grinding game rather than a shootout.

Availability tilts toward him on the back end. Cornerback Nate Wiggins (95% of snaps) and safety Jaylinn Hawkins (81%) are out, and Kyle Hamilton is questionable with a hip injury. That strips two or three regulars from the coverage that would contest his downfield throws. On his side, Herbert is questionable with a left middle finger injury that avoided a fracture. Losing guard Kayode Awosika thins an already 31st-ranked protection unit. McConkey's back is the biggest swing: he is Herbert's most efficient target, and without him more volume drifts toward the tight ends who have cost the offense all year.

keyMatchups.title: Herbert deep vs depleted Ravens coverage
keyMatchups.body: Baltimore is 26th on deep passes and allows 0.72 EPA per target to WR1s, and Wiggins and Hawkins are out. This is the game to push the ball outside to Johnston and McConkey. The risk is his interception habit on 10+ yard throws, which a thin secondary punishes less but doesn't erase.

keyMatchups.title: Short game into Baltimore's strength
keyMatchups.body: The Ravens rank 5th in short-pass EPA allowed, and the Chargers' underneath game is already their weakest passing area. If the plan is screens and tight end checkdowns again, expect another stalled day.

keyMatchups.title: Protection without Awosika
keyMatchups.body: Baltimore's 21st-ranked sack rate is the mildest rush he has faced in weeks. But his line ranks 31st in hits allowed and loses a guard who has played 69% of snaps. Whether he gets rid of the ball against an ordinary front will say a lot about how much of the sack problem is his.

nextGame.watch: Whether he attacks the Ravens' depleted secondary outside the numbers or settles into the checkdown-and-sack pattern of the last three games, and whether McConkey plays.

restOfSeason.body:
The parts most likely to improve are the ones furthest from his history. A 4.7% interception rate and a 2.6% TD rate are both well outside what six seasons say he is, and his red-zone accuracy (CPOE +1.0, 5 TDs, no picks) is fine. The extreme collapse in close fourth quarters rests on 28 plays and should soften. A realistic path has him around 185-230 passing yards a game with closer to one TD a week and the interceptions easing back.

What won't regress is the structure. The run game is the league's worst, the play-calling is the league's most run-heavy, and the protection ranks 31st and just lost a guard. His own pressure-to-sack rate has climbed for years. So sacks stay high, around 3.5 to 5 a game, and the ceiling stays capped. He averages under 200 passing yards a game and paces for 66 sacks. He will look like a league-average volume passer in a broken offense, not the top-10 producer of his past, unless the finger lingers or the line gets healthier.
swingFactors: McConkey's back and target distribution away from the tight ends
Whether the staff loosens its run-first lean

confidence.note: Eight consistent games of poor play conflict with a six-year positive track record. There are injury questions on him and his line, and several splits rest on small, high-leverage samples.
